transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-01-06 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~41 minutes
- Location: Zoom (recording)
- Attendees: Jared (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Lina (Redwood Solutions), Elliot (Sundog CTO), Priya (Head of Cloud), Marco (Platform Eng), Anika (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
Redwood intro and runtime capabilities; Sundog is an SI focused on regulated telematics workloads, interested in a hybrid onramp to offer GPU-backed LLM services to customers. Key constraints: VPC isolation, KMS choices, predictable latency SLOs, and cost targets. Action: Redwood to propose Dedicated trial + benchmark; send compliance docs; schedule deep technical VPC review.

Topics:
- Product fit: Redwood Dedicated vs Private deployment options
- Networking: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, egress controls
- Security: KMS/HSM, SOC2 evidence, SSO (SAML), audit logs
- Performance: latency targets, batch sizing, KV cache behavior
- Commercial framing: pilot scope, pricing, support levels

Transcript:
[00:00] Jared: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um this is Jared from Redwood, I'm the AE on this one. With me is Maya our SE and Lina on solutions. How are you all?
[00:10] Elliot: Good, thanks. Elliot here — CTO at Sundog. Appreciate you taking the time.
[00:15] Priya: Hi, Priya - head of cloud. We run most of our infra in a mix of AWS and a small on-prem footprint for regulated clients.
[00:22] Marco: Marco, platform eng. I'll be implementing the onramp bits.
[00:26] Anika: Anika, security. I'll be owning the compliance review.
[00:30] Maya: Awesome. Quick agenda — we want to understand your integration patterns, constraints, and what success looks like; we'll talk deployment options (hosted, dedicated, private), networking and security, and then propose next steps. Sound good?
[00:42] Elliot: Perfect. High level — Sundog is a systems integrator for telematics and finance verticals. We're seeing a lot of demand from customers who want generative features but need data residency and isolation. So we're evaluating partners to power a white-labeled LLM inference offering. Primary asks are: predictable latency, strong auditability, and ability to run in customers' VPCs or our managed VPCs.
[01:05] Jared: Great — thanks. Quick question about scale: are you thinking multi-tenant across customers on a shared cluster or spinning per-customer dedicated pools?
[01:15] Priya: Likely a mix. For lower-risk customers we'd run shared, but for regulated clients (financial) we need per-tenant isolation and in some cases on-prem deployment.
[01:25] Maya: Got it. For that mix, our typical pattern is Redwood Dedicated for managed per-tenant pools in your VPCs, and Redwood Private when you need full on-prem or air-gapped deployments. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity and the ability to pin model versions with isolation.
[01:40] Marco: When you say "in your VPCs" — how does that work network-wise?
[01:48] Maya: We support multiple patterns. For AWS we commonly do VPC peering for low-latency pathing, or PrivateLink if customers want a private endpoint without peering. We also have an edge connector for on-prem that tunnels to the control plane but keeps data path local if required. There are tradeoffs — peering is simpler for cross-AZ latency, PrivateLink simplifies routing and security posture.
[02:10] Anika: For our compliance we need encryption in transit and at rest, obviously. What KMS options do you support? We have requirements to use customer-managed KMS/HSM for certain clients.
[02:21] Lina: We integrate with AWS KMS and have options for customer-managed keys; for HSMs we can support BYOH with some additional setup — we can share the integration doc.
[02:30] Elliot: Another thing — latency. Our customers target p95 < 350ms for 1k token responses. How does Redwood perform?
[02:38] Maya: Typical numbers vary by model and sequence length. For quantized models on A100 equivalent, median token latency can be sub-20ms but end-to-end for a 1k token generation is often in the 200–500ms range depending on batching. We can tune batching and prefix caching to hit lower p95s.
[02:55] Marco: Does your runtime support prefix/KV cache sharing? If we have multi-turn chat sessions for a fleet of vehicles, we need to avoid recomputing large prompts every time.
[03:05] Maya: Yes, we have KV cache management and prefix caching with LRU policies; it can be pinned per-tenant to improve reuse. Worth noting cache hit behavior depends on how you partition sessions; we'll show logs in the console.
[03:20] Priya: On cost — our customers are price-sensitive. Any guidance on per-token costs for Dedicated vs Private?
[03:27] Jared: Costing interplay — Dedicated is usage-backed with reserved capacity; you get predictable throughput and pricing benefits over hosted when utilization is high. Private (on-prem) is a license + infra cost. We'll send a starter rate card and a sample TCO model for a couple of utilization scenarios.
[03:42] Elliot: Sounds good. Security audits are critical — do you have SOC2 Type II?
[03:48] Lina: Redwood has SOC2 Type II and we can share the report under NDA. We also keep audit logs per request with token-level traces.
[03:57] Anika: For those logs, do you persist PII by default? We need to ensure we can set retention windows and mask or not store payloads.
[04:06] Maya: You can configure retention and redact fields. For Dedicated and Private we offer more granular controls where logs can be stored in your S3 or on-prem logging stack.
[04:16] Marco: Great. Operationally, if we spin up a Dedicated pool in our VPC, how is autoscaling handled? We have spiky workloads from batch inference and streaming telematics.
[04:26] Maya: Our Dedicated controller supports configured autoscaling policies and burst capacity. You can set target throughput, min/max GPUs, and burst allowance. We also support graceful degradation and fallback to lower-cost model variants during peak.
[04:38] Elliot: Can we run a pilot with a small set of customers to measure latency and cost?
[04:43] Jared: Absolutely — typical pilot is a 2–4 week Dedicated reservation with a benchmarking plan. Maya will run the perf plan, we provide instrumentation, and Lina will help map the audit/compliance artifacts.
[04:56] Maya: I'll draft a benchmark plan. It'll include synthetic load, a sample of your real prompts, and KV-cache warmup scenarios. We'll define success criteria: p95 < 400ms for 1k tokens for the priority customer, and cost per 1k tokens under your target.
[05:12] Priya: One more thing on network egress — many of our customers demand no egress to public internet. If we use an edge connector or PrivateLink, can we ensure egress is limited?
[05:22] Maya: Yes — PrivateLink keeps traffic on AWS network; the edge connector can be configured to restrict external egress. For Private deployments, there is zero external egress if air-gapped. We should map this to each customer's requirements.
[05:33] Marco: What about model updating and rollouts? We want control over which model version is used per-tenant.
[05:39] Lina: You can pin a model version per deployment and manage rollouts with canary and automatic fallback policies. The console supports per-route config and model weighting.
[05:48] Elliot: Ok, more on the technical side — our stack is mostly Kubernetes on EKS. How does your runtime integrate with k8s clusters for on-prem?
[05:56] Maya: For on-prem or self-managed, we provide a helm chart that installs the runtime components and a control-plane connector. We also support a fully managed Private control plane if you want minimal ops. There are kernel-level optimizations for the inference runtime — we can talk about CUDA/ROCm compatibility in the deep technical call.
[06:15] Marco: Are there known constraints around CUDA versions? We have some customers on older CUDA stacks.
[06:20] Maya: We recommend certain CUDA versions for optimal kernels; older versions can work but may lack some optimizer code paths. We'll catalog supported hardware and drivers in the docs.
[06:29] Priya: For the pilot, can we get an A/B between your quantized model and an FP16 baseline to check quality vs cost?
[06:36] Maya: Yes, we can provision a quantized profile and a FP16 baseline. We'll include evaluation harness and metric collection so you can assess output quality differences.
[06:45] Anika: On identity — SSO. Our org uses SAML and we need RBAC integration for tenant admins.
[06:51] Lina: We support SAML and OIDC. RBAC is hierarchical — org, tenant, route-level permissions. We'll send a mapping doc for roles.
[07:01] Elliot: Any talk of resale/partner margins? If Sundog is reselling Redwood-backed inference to customers, would there be a partner pricing program?
[07:08] Jared: We do have partner programs — there's a reseller margin and a technical enablement package. We can surface partner commercial options once we have an initial pilot scope.
[07:17] Marco: Practical question — how does the fallback policy work under capacity pressure? Does it degrade to a smaller model or queue?
[07:23] Maya: Both options — you configure fallback to a compatible smaller model or to a queued/limited mode. We also have smart routing to send traffic to other regions or burst capacity if available.
[07:34] Priya: For telemetry and observability, can we export metrics to Prometheus and traces to Jaeger?
[07:40] Lina: Yes, we export metrics; we have a Prometheus endpoint and trace hooks compatible with OpenTelemetry.
[07:47] Elliot: Great. Can you walk through a rough timeline for pilot to production?
[07:51] Jared: Typical flow: week 0 — align on success criteria and sign pilot statement; week 1–2 — provision Dedicated pilot and run benchmarks; week 3 — iterate on tuning and security review; week 4 — decision point for expansion. That can compress if both sides prioritize.
[08:10] Anika: We'll need to run legal and DPAs — any restrictions in your standard terms around data processing?
[08:16] Lina: We have standard DPA templates and can negotiate data residency and processing terms; for certain regulated customers we do additional controls under enterprise agreements.
[08:26] Marco: For pilot provisioning, what's needed from our side network-wise? VPC CIDR, peering setup, security groups?
[08:33] Maya: We'll ask for a minimal list: VPC ID, peering permissions or PrivateLink endpoint creation ability, minimal security group rules for the connector, and an IAM role for provisioning (limited). We'll provide a checklist.
[08:47] Priya: Is there a way to test cost impact before committing — like a model simulator?
[08:52] Jared: We have a cost modeler spreadsheet that can simulate token throughput and GPU hours; we'll share it. Combined with the benchmark results you'll get a realistic TCO.
[09:01] Elliot: Any compliance red flags we should know about for telco data?
[09:05] Anika: Mostly around retention, encryption, and access controls. If we can push logs to our S3 and enforce KMS keys, that covers the main case.
[09:13] Maya: We can support pushing audit logs to your S3 with customer-managed KMS and support for access logging.
[09:19] Jared: Okay let's surface the immediate next steps: we'll send the onboarding deck, the pilot SOW template, compliance artifacts, and a benchmark plan. Maya, you'll lead the technical deep-dive.
[09:31] Maya: Yep, I'll draft the benchmark and propose dates for next week.
[09:35] Priya: One ask — can you include an example of a minimal infra diagram for Private vs Dedicated? Our architects want to see that.
[09:43] Lina: We'll include both diagrams and a short decision matrix.
[09:47] Marco: Cool. A couple of quick clarifying Qs — how are tenant quotas enforced? Is it at model route level?
[09:53] Maya: Quotas are enforced per API key/tenant at the route level; we also support burst allowances and throttling policies.
[10:00] Elliot: Any references you can share for other SI partners doing similar onramps?
[10:05] Jared: We can share anonymized case studies — I'll include a partner one-pager.
[10:09] Anika: For the SOC2 report, we'll need to get it under NDA.
[10:13] Lina: Understood — we'll send an NDA link and then the report.
[10:17] Priya: Ok I think that's the bulk. Anything else from you, Redwood?
[10:21] Jared: Not from me. Quick note — we can also offer a short enablement workshop for your sales and engineering folks to speed time-to-first-byte.
[10:29] Elliot: That would be useful.
[10:31] Maya: I'll add that as an optional item in the follow-up.
[10:34] Jared: Great. Let's recap.
